summary: Defines MIB objects for managing SNMP agents that use the AgentX protocol, so the extensible agent setup can itself be monitored. It is a standards-track document at the draft standard level.

eli5.summary: This lets you check on the helper desk system itself, like a dashboard for the helpers.

questions: what is an snmp master agent and subagent
how to close an agentx subagent session
subtitle: A MIB that lets a network manager see which subagents are plugged into an SNMP master agent, and what each one handles.

tldr.problem: AgentX splits one SNMP agent into a master agent and several subagents, but a manager had no standard way to see which subagents are connected or which parts of the MIB each one serves.
tldr.mechanism: The AGENTX-MIB module, implemented by the master agent, exposes tables of transport connections, sessions and registered MIB regions, plus a few general settings such as the default timeout.
tldr.outcome: Managers can inspect the extensible agent and, optionally, close a subagent session by setting one read-write object. The module is a Draft Standard.

today: RFC 2742 is a Draft Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the MIB module that goes with the AgentX protocol in RFC 2741.

sections.title: Why an AgentX MIB Is Needed
sections.content:
The SNMP Agent Extensibility Protocol (AgentX, see RFC 2741) spreads the work of one SNMP agent across a single master agent and multiple subagents. This memo defines the AGENTX-MIB module, which describes that arrangement so it can be managed with ordinary SNMP.

The goals listed in the RFC are to list the subagent connections that have logical sessions open with the master agent, to identify each connection's transport address and type, and to identify each session's vendor, AgentX protocol version and other characteristics. It also covers which MIB objects each session implements, in what context and at what priority, and protocol parameters such as response timeouts. Managers are allowed, but not required, to close subagent sessions explicitly.

The module is written in SMIv2, and the abstract says it is semantically identical to the peer SMIv1 definitions. The MIB module will be implemented by the master agent.
sections.eli5: When many helpers share one help desk, somebody needs to be able to ask who is working right now and what they cover. This document is that list.

sections.title: Four Groups and Three Tables
sections.content:
The MIB sits at { mib-2 74 } and is organized into four groups. agentxGeneral describes the master agent's AgentX support, including the protocol version. agentxConnection describes the current connections able to carry AgentX sessions. agentxSession describes the current sessions, and agentxRegistration describes the current registrations.

Three tables form the heart of the module: the connection, session and registration tables. They are tied together by shared indices. Many registration entries belong to one session, many session entries belong to one connection, and many registration entries belong to one connection. The links are expressed through agentxSessionIndex and agentxConnIndex.
sections.eli5: There are three lists, one inside the other: roads (connections), trips on a road (sessions), and the stops each trip handles (registrations). Each list entry carries the numbers that tell you which road and trip it belongs to.

sections.title: The Connection and Session Tables
sections.content:
A row in the connection table describes one AgentX transport connection. A row is created when a new transport connection is established and destroyed when it ends. There may be zero, one or more sessions on a connection. Each row records the open time, the transport domain (agentxConnTransportDomain) and the remote subagent address (agentxConnTransportAddress). That address may be zero-length for unix-domain sockets, since the subagent need not bind a filename to its local socket. The index agentxConnIndex should not be re-used and stays constant for the life of the connection.

A row in the session table is created when a session is successfully established. It is destroyed when the transport connection ends or the session is closed. It records values taken from the open request: an object identifier (agentxSessionObjectID, reported as 0.0 by subagents that lack the notion), a text description, the AgentX version of the session (which must not exceed the master agent's version) and a timeout in seconds. A timeout of zero means the master agent's default is used.

The session table is indexed by connection index plus session index. The session index is the same as h.sessionID in the AgentX header, may be zero, and should not be re-used after a session closes.
sections.eli5: Each connection is like a phone line to a helper. Each session is one conversation on that line, and the table notes who is on the line, how long ago they called, and how long you will wait for an answer.

sections.title: Registrations, Priorities and Timeouts
sections.content:
The registration table lists the regions of the MIB that sessions have registered. An entry appears when a session registers a region. It disappears when the region is unregistered, the session closes or the connection closes. Entries are indexed by connection index, session index and agentxRegIndex.

Each entry gives the context (a zero-length context means the default context), the starting object identifier of the region (inclusive), and optional range fields. When agentxRegRangeSubId is non-zero, it names the sub-identifier of the starting identifier that is replaced by agentxRegUpperBound to form the region's upper bound. The entry also records the priority, a timeout and whether the registration was an instance registration.

Lower priority values mean higher priority, and sessions should use 127 when they want a default. Timeouts nest: a registration timeout overrides the session timeout, which overrides the system-wide agentxDefaultTimeout (default 5 seconds), and a value of zero at a lower level means fall through to the next level up.
sections.eli5: Each helper puts a claim on part of the big book of answers. If two helpers claim the same page, the one with the lower number goes first, and timeouts say how long to wait before giving up on a helper.

sections.title: Compliance and Closing Sessions
sections.content:
Almost everything in the module is read-only. The one exception is agentxSessionAdminStatus, which can be up(1) or down(2). Setting it to down(2) closes the subagent session, with the close reason set to reasonByManager.

The module's compliance statement requires the object group containing all accessible objects. It states that a compliant agent can implement every object in the module as read-only, so write access to agentxSessionAdminStatus is not required.
sections.eli5: You can look at nearly everything but not change it. The only button you may press hangs up on one helper, and even that button is optional.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points out that the single read-write object, agentxSessionAdminStatus, may be sensitive in some environments. Allowing SET operations without proper protection can hurt network operations, and setting the object to an inappropriate value can prevent access to management information or give access to information that should not be available.

It therefore recommends controlling even GET access and possibly encrypting values sent over the network. SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, even on a secured network, and implementers are advised to consider SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). Configuring the SNMP entity so that only legitimate principals can read or change these objects is left to the user.
sections.eli5: The hang-up button could cause trouble if the wrong person pressed it, so the RFC says to lock the control panel and let only trusted people in.
